What DORA actually requires of your CI/CD pipelines

DORA requires demonstrable operational resilience, which for CI/CD means evidenced control over who and what can change production, provable integrity of the build, and tested recovery. In practice that comes down to removing shared long-lived credentials, signing artefacts, recording provenance, and proving you can rebuild and recover on demand.

The numbers

  • Evidence DORA is satisfied by proof, not by good intentions
  • Provenance you must be able to show what shipped and who changed it
  • Tested recovery untested backups do not count

What is DORA really asking of a pipeline?

Strip the legal language and DORA asks three operational questions. Can you prove who and what can change production? Can you prove the integrity of what you ship? Can you recover when something breaks, and have you tested that? Everything else is detail hanging off those three.

Where do teams fall short?

Almost always on identity and integrity. Pipelines authenticate with shared, long-lived credentials that nobody can attribute to a person or a job; artefacts ship unsigned with no provenance; and recovery has never actually been rehearsed. The first of those is exactly what our secrets and vault engineering removes, replacing shared secrets with short-lived, attributable credentials.

What does a compliant pipeline look like?

Every change is attributable to a verified identity, every artefact is signed and carries provenance, and recovery is a tested runbook rather than a hope. Where machine identity is the weak point, our PKI and machine identity engineering gives each workload a verifiable identity instead of a shared password.

How do you get there without a two-year programme?

Start with a scored gap analysis. Our Secrets and Pipeline Security Assessment maps your current pipeline against these requirements and returns a prioritised 90-day plan, so you close the highest-risk gaps first and can show a regulator a credible trajectory.
